header.tag_why: The rep places the turn at a customer engineer's unprompted weekend prototype built with our docs and sandbox, after which Daniel stopped saying "if"; the marketplace capabilities (onboarding sitters, identity checks, local-currency pay) also landed but did not mark the turning point.

messaging_changes.current_line: Built for developers: launch payments fast with our APIs, docs and sandbox.
messaging_changes.change: For engineering-led buyers, make the developer claim an early ask: invite one of their engineers to build their own core payment flow (for a pet-sitting app, sitter pay) in our sandbox using our docs, then review it with their engineering lead. Suggested line: "Don't take our word for it. Have one of your engineers build your own payment flow in our sandbox this week."
messaging_changes.why: The deal turned when a customer engineer built a working sitter payment flow over a weekend with our docs and sandbox, after which Daniel "stopped saying "if"", so the proof was hands-on experience rather than our claim.

messaging_changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
messaging_changes.change: For buyers whose engineering team carries payments upkeep, open with removing the burden, in the customer's words: "Payments shouldn't be a team." Follow with: stop tying up engineers just keeping payments working, and get stalled roadmap items like faster sitter pay moving. Make paying people locally in new countries the second beat. Use the buyer's own nouns ("sitter pay", not "payouts").
messaging_changes.why: Expansion set the deadline, but the pain the signer felt was two engineers "just keeping sitter payments working" and a sitter-pay roadmap item pushed three quarters, which the customer framed as "We want to stop babysitting this."

messaging_changes.change: For buyers switching providers, add a migration proof point ready before the competitor raises it: a named customer at comparable scale that moved saved cards without losses, plus a direct, confirmed answer on keeping PayPal and Venmo. It must answer the buyer's question as asked: "who's done this at our size without losing cards?"
messaging_changes.why: After the Braintree call the conversation went from "how fast can we build this" to "what do we lose". The rep "danced around" PayPal, had no Venmo answer, and never sent the saved-card reference the customer asked for.

messaging_changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
messaging_changes.change: Stop leading with the acceptance-rate slide for buyers with low average transaction values who say auth rates aren't a concern. Ask first whether authorization rates are a problem for them, and show this only if the answer is yes.
messaging_changes.why: The rep ran the whole acceptance-rate slide to silence, and the decider said "our average booking is 38 dollars, I'm not losing sleep over auth rates."

trigger.insight: Expansion set the deadline, but the pain was engineering drag: two engineers kept busy just holding sitter payments together and a sitter-pay roadmap item slipping three quarters running. M1's grow-globally framing speaks to the expansion and ignores the burden, which is the part the signer actually felt. The source of the two-engineers figure is not stated, so treat it as the rep's account.
trigger.messaging: For marketplace-style buyers led by engineering, open with taking payments maintenance off the engineering team and unblocking the sitter-pay roadmap, and make local-currency expansion the second beat.

competitor.insight: The customer's complaint about the competitor was relationship churn, not product. After the Braintree call, the buying conversation moved from speed to loss: PayPal, Venmo and saved cards. What Braintree actually said is unknown, but the effect was to make switching feel risky. We won despite that shift, not because we answered it.
competitor.messaging: Prepare a loss-aversion answer up front (what you keep: PayPal, Venmo, saved cards) and contrast relationship continuity with account-manager churn, since M5's tiered response times does not speak to that complaint.

message.insight: M2 won, but as a hands-on experience, not as a claim: the proof was their own engineer's working flow, not our slide. M4 died on contact because the buyer did not see authorization rates as his problem, and the rep ran the whole slide anyway. The reaction to the marketplace capabilities is the rep's read, with no customer words attached.
message.messaging: Replace the M2 claim with an invitation to build their own core flow (here, sitter pay) in the sandbox, and drop M4 from the default deck for buyers who say auth rates aren't a concern.

decided.insight: The deciding moment happened without us and without us knowing about it, so as things stand it is luck, not a repeatable motion. The observable signal was the decider's language: he stopped saying "if" once an internal engineer had proven the build.
decided.messaging: Make an engineer-built prototype of the customer's core flow an explicit early step in the pitch, so the moment that won this deal is something we ask for rather than wait for.

gaps.insight: The rep called this "a clean one", but three gaps stayed open: a deferred PayPal answer, no Venmo answer even now, and a saved-card reference that was promised and never sent. These are exactly the loss questions that appeared after the Braintree call. The customer's engineer saying "we'll find out" at kickoff means the migration risk moved into implementation rather than being resolved, and generic M8 customer stories did not answer a request for a peer at their size.
gaps.messaging: Build a migration proof pack with a named reference that moved saved cards without losses at comparable scale, plus a crisp PayPal and Venmo continuity answer, and use it in place of generic M8 customer stories.

language.insight: The customer describes the problem as a burden to get rid of (haunted house, babysitting, a team that shouldn't exist), not as a growth opportunity. Their outcome is a promise to sitters, "paid by Friday". Our vocabulary (marketplace, payouts, sellers, in M11) is not theirs: they say "the app" and "sitter pay".
language.messaging: Lead with the burden-removal frame (payments shouldn't need a team) and mirror the customer's own nouns for the people they pay and when, e.g. sitters "paid by Friday", instead of "pay out to sellers".

close.rep_takeaway: This deal was won by a customer engineer in our sandbox, not by the deck, and nobody on our side knew it was happening. Next time, ask early for an engineer to build their own core flow, and stay close enough to know when they do. Also, a deal is not "clean" while a promised reference is unsent and the Venmo answer is unknown: close those loops before kickoff, because they come back in implementation.
